Purpose:

You are being asked to participate in a research study being conducted by Dr. Simon Howard at the University of Miami, Dr. Hongbo Yu & Ava Ma de Sousa at the University of California, Santa Barbara.  Participation is voluntary. The purpose of this research study is to investigate how people’s life experiences influence their thoughts, perception and behavior. At the end of the survey, you will receive more detailed information about the purpose of this research.



Procedures:

If you choose to be in the study, you will complete an online survey. The survey will take about 30 minutes to complete.



Confidentiality:

The researcher will not know your name, and no identifying information will be connected to your survey answers in any way. The survey is therefore anonymous. However, if you are taking this survey through CloudResearch, your account is associated with a number that the researcher has to be able to see in order to pay you, and in some cases these numbers are associated with public profiles which could, in theory, be searched. For this reason, though the researcher will not be looking at anyone’s public profiles, the fact of your participation in the research (as opposed to your actual survey responses) is technically considered “confidential” rather than truly anonymous.



Costs/Payments:

If you are enrolling through SONA, you will be given 1 credit per half hour of participation in this study. For participants recruited through Cloud Research, you will be given $5.00 for your participation. For participants recruited through avenues besides these, participation will be on a voluntary basis without monetary compensation.



If you withdraw from the study early, you are eligible to receive partial credits for the time you have participated (e.g., 0.5 credits, $2.5) upon contacting the researcher at avamadesousa@ucsb.edu.



Contact Information:         

​ If you have questions about the research, please contact Dr. Simon Howard, Assistant Professor of Psychology in the Department of Psychology, via email at simon.howard@miami.edu or Ava Ma de Sousa at avamadesousa@ucsb.edu





If you have any questions regarding your rights as a research subject, please contact the Human Subjects Committee at (805) 893-3807 or hsc@research.ucsb.edu. Or write to the University of California, Human Subjects Committee, Office of Research, Santa Barbara, CA 93106-2050



You may also contact the Human Subject Research Office at the University of Miami. Please call the HSRO at 305-243-3195 if you are a participant in any research being conducted by UM, and:

	You cannot reach the research team.

	You have questions about your rights as a research subject.

When my roommate (Indian) tried to engage with another girl (white), the girl entirely ignored my roommate and pretended she didn't exist. I was appalled at this behavior. I am a white woman myself and I could not believe that the girl chose to treat my roommate that way. So neither of us joined the club water polo team.

During COVID-19 there was a lot of hatred and racism against Chinese people. It happened especially towards the beginning of 2020 but has continued on even until now. It was particularly impactful because it was directed toward people of my racial background.

We were at the market and it was any regular day. However, this quickly made me realize that there are a lot of people who view Hispanic people in a negative way and openly voice rude things.
It is the most hurtful when it concerns my parents such as the change in people's tone when they hear my parents accent.

When I was in my junior year of high school, and becoming more radicalized the more I learned about politics, my dad had gotten laid off another job (the second in the span of three years) seemingly out of nowhere. We were running low on funds and he spent a lot of his time being stressed about how to make ends meet. He got in contact with an old friend who put in a good word for him at an insurance company he had sought a job from a year or two prior, and went into the interview feeling incredibly confident. He was the most qualified person there and the interviewers really seemed to connect with him. The following week, the company hires someone else with less experience and no real friend or family connection within the company to account for that. My dad was wracking his head trying to understand how he wasn't selected, as was the friend who had sent him there in the first place. When he told me about it, I asked him who they hired instead, and he told me it was a white woman. My dad was born in England and immigrated here when he was 12 with his family, but he is Indian and wears a turban with his business attire for religious reasons. He has an American accent, but has brown skin. Functionally, he's just like any other American, except incredibly qualified in his field. On the surface, however, he's an Indian guy with a big headpiece. The panel was all white. My dad happens to be very conservative, but when I pointed this out to him, I saw first the instinct to deny that it was racism, then thinking critically about the situation, and then he admitted out loud that I was probably right. That's the only time he's ever admitted to being subjected to racial prejudice. Conservative Indians often think that admitting to issues of discrimination will make white people like them less, so they suppress those feelings for the sake of being accepted a little more. Hearing my dad finally admit it out loud wasn't the thing that radicalized me or made me realize racism is bad, but it did make me far more passionate about dismantling racist and bigoted institutions in America.

She was walking to her car after buying groceries, when a lady who was headed towards the store called her a "N*ger" as she walked past her. This was particularly impactful to me because of how uncalled for this action was. She was simply doing her day-to-day activities when this lady just decided to use racial slurs just because she wanted to.

I was thinking then that until all parties can walk past the concept of rights, wrongs, and race, it just doesn't seem like racial and ethnic equality and fairness seems possible. My sister, my dad, and myself were heading up to drop her off at her university after visiting home. We stopped half way through for a meal and ended up in restaurant that had primarily white customers, while I noticed it, I didn't think much of it at first. When we were seated, my sister had noticed an elderly white couple glancing over at us from time to time. Although I'm unsure why that might've been, my guess is always that it was likely because we were speaking Spanish which is what we usually do since it's our first language. Even after our food was served the couple was still glancing at us, and seemed to continue and mock my dad when he was holding his fork with his fist. It was only after my sister very loudly cleared her throat at the couple (as if to confront them) that they stopped staring at us for the rest of the night. I wasn't aware that this had happened until after we had left the restaurant. This was about 3 or 4 years ago, but is a memory I still think about every now and then. It makes me frustrated and angry that I didn't realize what was going on and wasn't able to do something to prevent it. It makes me grateful that my sister was there to keep them in check. But mostly, it makes me sad thinking about my dad who had no idea what was going on. It makes me think about how this might happen to him often without realizing or how it small microaggressions such as this are unfortunately extremely often and all around us. It makes me wonder why some people are so hateful towards a stranger, and makes me determined to help make a difference.

I can share that racism is a significant and pervasive issue that has been widely documented and discussed in various contexts, including historical events, media, and personal accounts shared by individuals.  For many people, instances of racism can be particularly impactful when they involve direct personal experiences or when they highlight systemic inequalities. For example, the murder of George Floyd in 2020 was a pivotal moment that sparked global protests and conversations about racial injustice and police brutality. This event was impactful because it brought widespread attention to the ongoing issues of racial discrimination and violence faced by Black communities.  Another example might be hearing personal stories from friends or family members who have experienced racism, such as being unfairly treated in the workplace, facing discrimination in educational settings, or encountering racial slurs and microaggressions in daily life. These stories can be impactful because they highlight the personal and emotional toll that racism takes on individuals and communities.

I first became deeply aware of the real impact of racism during my high school years at an international school in Taiwan. Our school prided itself on diversity, with students from all over the world, yet even in this environment, I witnessed moments that made me reflect on the subtle but powerful ways racism exists.  One of the most impactful moments occurred during a group project in history class. We were discussing immigration and cultural identity, and a classmate—who was of African descent—shared his experiences of facing discrimination when traveling. He recounted how airport security singled him out for extra screening nearly every time he traveled, how people would stare at him in public spaces, and how he had even been called offensive names in certain countries. As he spoke, I noticed some classmates dismissing his words, with one even saying, "Maybe they were just being extra careful. You’re probably overthinking it."  I felt uncomfortable. Here was someone bravely sharing his experiences, yet instead of listening, some classmates were invalidating his reality. I had always thought of our school as a place where students embraced different backgrounds, but this moment showed me that even in diverse environments, ignorance and bias can exist in subtle ways.  Later that day, I talked to him privately, expressing that I believed him and wanted to understand more. He appreciated it, saying that sometimes the hardest part of experiencing racism isn’t just the incident itself, but having people dismiss it afterward.  This experience made me realize how important it is to listen to and validate others’ experiences. It also made me reflect on my own privilege—though I had faced certain challenges as an international student, I had never experienced the level of racial profiling or discrimination that others had. Since then, I have made it a point to educate myself, challenge biases, and speak up when I see discrimination, whether online or in real life.  This moment reshaped my perspective and deepened my awareness of how racism persists in different forms, even in seemingly open-minded spaces.

I also witnessed this hatred in the comments of almost every social media post even relating in some way to Judaism or any Jewish person, and this was years ago. In the last year and a half, these online experiences have turned into real life ones. Coming to college directly after the year of October 7th meant this topic was even more prevalent on campuses. My friends and people in my on-campus Jewish community have received countless instances of hatred, threats, and displays of violence or vandalization even when they were simply existing as Jewish people at UCSB. column269: One of the most impactful instances of racism I’ve seen in recent years has been the increase in hateful attacks and ICE raids targeting Hispanic communities. column269: The Black Lives Matter movement was especially impactful, as because so many people were on social media during quarantine, the transition from empty roads to loaded, hopeful streets filled with signs from people of al ethnicities and cultures supporting Black Lives Matter made me feel hopeful in the equality of all cultures and ethnicities for the future, feeling like we were moving forward as a society during this movement. My sister's running friend is Asian, and her father's life was taken away in a shooting at a Taiwanese Presbyterian Church, while trying to protect someone else. His family talked about him and his heroic efforts as a father, doctor, and human. I forgot to mention this in the polls, but when my mom told me about this, which happened May 15 of 2022, my entire family and I broke down. My mom and sister who knows their family best, had previously known them for around seven years already, as my sister and their family's daughter had traveled and ran together for track and cross country. Dr. John Cheng loved talking with my mom while their daughters ran together and grew up together, and our families were close because of this. The day that I came home from school, and my mom toldd my sisters and I about what happened, I genuinely could not believe it. I felt broken. I felt empty. When the high school held a ceremony for Dr. John Cheng, I cried the entire time. I never ran with my sister and Dr. John Cheng's daughter, but I knew how good of people the entire family was, and continue to be. Ultimately, what I realize with racism is that people disregard people as human beings, that these people have a life, a heart, meaning, family, friends, and hope. Why does it matter what someone looks like, what they worship, or where they come from? Why are we dividing ourselves? At that ceremony, Dr. John Cheng's wife, one of my mom's best friends, acknowledged how Dr. John Cheng, even when he realized a shooting was happening, attempted to disarm the shooter, attempting to protect everyone in the church. His life was taken away, while he was trying to save others. I will always have this engraved in my mind. As kind, and as loving as one can be, their life can be taken away because of their race, ethnicity, culture, and beliefs.
